question: Updated rules are changing the Generalised Scheme of Preferences. The scheme lets developing countries export goods to the EU with low or zero tariffs, with the aim of eradicating poverty and integrating them into the world economy. In order to benefit from preferences, participating countries have to ratify international conventions on human rights and the environment added to the agreements by the EU.

To protect European rice production, a safeguard clause has been included that blocks imports beyond a certain limit, but producers say the clause fails to go far enough to prevent unfair competition from certain third countries such as Myanmar and Cambodia. The conditions set out in the agreement provide for the activation of the clause when the amount exceeds 561 tonnes. Italy boasts 56.
7 % of the European growing area and is the leading European producer with around 1.4 billion kg of rice per year, which amounts to over 50 % of EU production.

In view of the above, can the Commission clarify how it intends to demonstrate that this threshold is not excessively high and that third countries – which are often far from complying with our environmental and health standards – are not being protected to the detriment of the European rice sector and without any thought being given to the serious risk of unfair competition?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.2.2026) The co-legislators agreed on the political elements of the new Generalised Scheme Preferences (GSP) Regulation on 1 December 20251. Currently, this brings certainty and predictability to 65 developing countries and also to EU companies.

As regards rice, the GSP regulation fully recognises the importance of the EU rice production: (i) Rice is defined as sensitive product, without tariff preferences for all standard GSP and GSP+ beneficiary countries.

Only Least Developed Countries, such as Cambodia and Myanmar, benefit from tariff preferences when exporting rice to the EU; (ii) There are three different safeguard mechanisms (general safeguards, special safeguards and the special surveillance mechanism) which also apply to the EU rice sector, if the relevant conditions are met, and support the viability of the EU rice sector and the smooth functioning of the market; (iii) There will be a new, fully automatic safeguard mechanism, only for rice, if the conditions are met.

This is the result of two years of negotiations between the co-legislators, after careful consideration of the positions of both institutions and of relevant stakeholders, including the rice sector. Beyond GSP rules, any food product imported in the EU market must comply with the EU’s sanitary and phytosanitary requirements. This is not negotiable.

Moreover, the EU Vision for Agriculture2 will strive toward fairer global level playing field for agriculture. The Commission also works to strengthen control on imports and will establish a principle that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU are not allowed for imported products. Additionally, for the next two years the Commission announced a 50% increase in the number of audits carried outside EU.
